data.title: Combination Sum IV
data.summary:
Input: A list of distinct integers nums and an integer target.
Output: The number of possible combinations that add up to the target.
Rules: The order of elements in a combination matters, meaning (1, 2) and (2, 1) are distinct. Elements can be reused.
constraints: All elements in nums are unique

data.generator_code:
def generate(rng, n):
    target = max(1, n)
    size = rng.randint(1, min(10, n))
    nums = sorted(list(set(rng.randint(1, 10) for _ in range(size))))
    return [nums, target]

def generate_worst(rng, n):
    target = n
    nums = [1]
    return [nums, target]

data.key_insight: Since the order of elements matters, this is a permutation problem rather than a combination problem. We can define `dp[i]` as the number of possible combinations that add up to `i`. For each sum from 1 to target, the number of ways to reach `i` is the sum of `dp[i - num]` for each `num` in `nums`.

steps.title: Initialize DP table
steps.detail: Create a list `dp` of size `target + 1` initialized to 0, with `dp[0] = 1` because there is exactly one way to make a sum of 0 (by choosing nothing).

steps.title: Iterate through all possible sums
steps.detail: Loop `i` from 1 up to `target` to compute the number of combinations for each sub-target.

steps.title: Transition using each number in nums
steps.detail: For each `i`, iterate through every `num` in `nums`. If `i >= num`, add `dp[i - num]` to `dp[i]`.

steps.title: Return the result
steps.detail: Return `dp[target]` which holds the total number of combinations to reach the target.

data.pattern_summary: Dynamic programming is used when a problem can be broken down into overlapping subproblems with optimal substructure. You reach for it when you need to count total ways or find optimal values without recomputing the same states.

pattern_options.name: Dynamic Programming (Bottom-Up)
pattern_options.feedback: Correct. We can build the answer for the target up from smaller sums to avoid redundant recursive calls.

pattern_options.name: Two pointers
pattern_options.feedback: Two pointers work on sorted linear data for pairs or windows, not for counting all valid nested combinations that sum to a target.

pattern_options.name: Greedy
pattern_options.feedback: Greedy choices make locally optimal decisions, but counting all possible combinations requires exploring multiple valid paths.

pattern_options.name: Binary search
pattern_options.feedback: Binary search requires sorted data to eliminate half the search space per step, which does not apply here.

signals.hint: Implies counting total valid paths or states rather than finding just one.
Means the same subproblem states will be visited multiple times across different branches.

data.brute_force_idea: Use depth-first search to recursively subtract each number in nums from the target until the remaining sum hits zero or goes below zero.
data.brute_force_why: At each step, we branch out by every number in nums, leading to an exponential number of recursive calls.
data.bottleneck: The recursive function recalculates the exact same remaining sums multiple times across different branches, resulting in massive wasted work.
bottleneck_hints: Look at how many times dfs is called with the same argument.
Draw out the recursion tree for target equals 4 with nums equal to [1, 2, 3] and notice repeating subtrees.
Think about how you could store the result of a subproblem once solved so you never compute it twice.

events.label: Coach: why the complexity is what it is

data.insight: The brute force approach recomputes the number of combinations for the same remaining target repeatedly in separate branches of the recursion tree. The bottom-up dynamic programming approach eliminates this redundant work by building up the answer from 1 to the target iteratively, storing previously calculated combination counts in an array so each subproblem is solved exactly once.

derivation.note: Allocates and initializes the dp array of size target + 1.
The outer loop runs target times, iterating through every integer from 1 to target.
The inner loop runs nums.length (n) times for each step of the outer loop.
Performs a constant-time array lookup and addition.

data.time_summary: The outer loop runs target times, and the inner loop runs n times for every iteration of the outer loop. Multiplying these together yields O(target * n) total time, which is supported by the measured evidence where doubling the target roughly doubles the total step count.
data.space_summary: We allocate a single dp list of size target + 1 to store the number of combinations for each subproblem, resulting in O(target) extra space.
data.takeaway: When a problem asks for the number of ways to reach a target using reusable components where order matters, use a bottom-up DP array indexed by the target value.
mistakes: Forgetting to initialize dp[0] = 1, which acts as the base case for building larger combinations.
Using nested loops in the wrong order, which would calculate permutations incorrectly.
Failing to check if the current target value is greater than or equal to the number (i >= num) before reading from the dp table.

data.overview: Combination Sum IV calculates the total number of permutations that sum up to a target using dynamic programming. By iterating through every possible sum from 1 to target and summing up ways from valid previous states, we account for order-dependent combinations.
data.intuition: Think of building a staircase of height target. At each step, you can take strides corresponding to the numbers given in nums. The total ways to reach step i is simply the sum of the ways you could reach the steps from which you can take a single stride to land on i.

pitfalls: Confusing permutations with combinations and looping through nums in the outer loop instead of the inner loop.
Forgetting to set dp[0] = 1, which causes all subsequent subtarget values to remain 0.
Not handling edge cases where target is smaller than the smallest number in nums.
